 The Committee recommends that the renovation work of labour  room in LHMC 
and Smt. S.K. Hospital must be completed within current financial year 2022 -23. 
Expressing displeasure over the delay on major renovation of Padiatric Centre in 
Kalawari Saran Centre of Medical Sciences for children, the Committee hopes that 
approval for the proposal would be sought at the earliest so that the renovation work is 
commenced and completed within a set timeframe.  
(Para 3.11.4) 
VACANCY POSITION IN FIRST SIX AIIMS 
 The Committee takes into account the various steps taken by Ministr y to fill up 
the vacant faculty and non -faculty staff of first six AIIMS, however, despite plethora of 
steps, the vacancy position in various AIIMS is a matter of concern to the Committee.  
The Committee understands that the recruitment exercise is planned  by the respective 
management of the Institute, nevertheless , the Ministry cannot shrug off its 

63 
 
responsibility from monitoring the progress of recruitment process.  The Committee 
does not approve the plea of the Ministry that posts are filled upto the rang e of service 
already operational in the Institute, rather the reverse proposition is correct /true i.e 
many departments in various AIIMS remain inoperational due to vacant faculty and 
non-faculty staff.  The Committee, therefore, urges upon the Ministry to ensure 
adequate healthcare work force in all AIIMS like precious Institute not only for 
delivering the assured health services but for imparting education and undertaking 
research projects to understand the biology of various diseases.  
(Para 3.12.7) 
NATIONAL ORGAN TRANSPLANT PROGRAM (NOTP) 
 The Committee appreciates that despite lower allocation of budget to NOTP and 
underutilization of IEC fund the organ donation rate has increased from 0.16 in 2012 to 
0.52 in 2019 due to enhanced impetus to organ do nation awareness  campaign.  
However, the Committee observes that to make NOTP more effective and bridge the 
gap between demand and supply of the organs for transplantation , various new 
components have been incorporated in the programme viz. Medical Education for doing 
transplantation, training to transplants teams, setting up of 4 skills centers in NOTTO, 
10 Regional/State Bio-material centre, setting up of SOTTO in each State, strengthening 
existing retrieval and transplant centre etc.  The Committee, therefore, recommends the 
Ministry to assess whether the continuing quantum of budgetary grant would be 
sufficient to meet the expenditure involving on various activities enshrined in new 
components of NOTP. 
(Para 3.13.4) 
STATUS OF PROJECTS UNDERTAKEN BY AIIMS, DELHI 
 The Committee recommends that the Ministry must give green sig nal to the 
Master Plan of AIIMS, New Delhi, so that the cherished goal of developing AIIMS into 
a world class Medical University by March, 2024 can be achieved without fail.  The 
Committee further recommends that redevelopmen t of AIIMS Residential colonies   
Project should get clearance from NDMC without any delay so that civil work get 
commenced at the earliest and the project is completed within set timeframe.  The 
Committee, however, appreciates the efforts of AIIMS management and the Ministry 
for offering the nation one of the best healthcare facilities to the people of the country 
and even to people of neighbouring countries of India.  
(Para 3.14.3) 
VACANCY POSITION IN AIIMS, NEW DELHI 
 
 The Committee is constrained to note that despite necessary instruc tions being 
given by the Ministry to AIIMS, New Delhi to fill up the vacant posts, a total of 404 
Group-A Medical posts are vacant.  Similarly, 26.81% of Group -B and 20.73% of 
Group-C posts are vacant that must have bearing on delivery of health care facilities.  
The Committee, therefore, urges upon AIIMS Management and the Ministry to take 
concrete steps for filling up of vacant posts without further delay. 
(Para 3.15.3)

huge gap between the identification and acceptance of mental health illness i.e 
symptoms causing factors and its treatment.  Being an apex institute for mental health 
in the country, NIMHANS has the responsibility to reduce the burden of mental illness 
in the country. 
(Para 3.16.3) 
NORTH EASTERN INDIRA GANDHI REGIONAL INSTITUTE OF HEALTH AND

 The Committee is not happy to observe that the completion date for the 
construction projects in NEIGRIHM has further been extended from May/June, 2022 to

construction projects of Regional Cancer Centre under graduate medical college and 
expansion of Nursing College.  The Committee, therefore, recommends the Ministry to 
update the status of those projects and further instruct the NEIGRIHMs Management 
to keep vigil on Institute’s construction consultant M/s HSCC to ensure that 04 
remaining buildings out of 12 buildings are also completed within revised timeframe i.e 
September, 2022. 
(Para 3.17.3) 
AYUSHMAN BHARAT HEALTH-WELLNESS CENTRES (AB-HWCS) 
 The Committee appreciates the efforts made by the Ministry in operationalizing 
a total of 1,20,112 AB-HWCs throughout the country against the target of 1,50, 000 AB-
HWCs by December, 2022. The Committee, however, recommends that the Ministry 
will make all out effort to achieve the target of opratinalizing 1,50,000 AB -HWCs in 
order to provide Comprehens ive Primary Healthcare Services across the country.  The 
Committee further recommends that all these centre must have adequate human 
resource with 4 technical expertise and latest tools and techniques, diagnostic kits, 
medicines to provide quality healthca re service and standard treatment.  The 
Committee also recommends the Ministry should popularize tele -consultation Sundere-
Sanjeevani in rural areas.   
(Para 3.18.5) 
MERGER OF POOLS UNDER NHM 
 The Committee understands the merger of flexible pools will end ow greater 
flexibility to States and UTs for appropriation of funds on various component of the 
scheme as per the instant requirement, however, the Committee desire to be apprised of 
the achievement of physical target as a result of release of funds agains t various 
components/activities approved in SPIP and subsequent improvement in health 
indicators. The Committee further desires to know as how the scheme incesstinize 
States/UTs with poor health track record on health indicators. The Committee notes

various mode of keeping track on the financial utilization of fund and progress 
thereupon, however, such monitoring mechanism must oversee the transformation of 
healthcare delivery system at ground level , that is the ultimate measurement of success 
of the scheme.

The Committee desires that the pending 136 utilization certificate amounting to 
Rs. 629.69 crore with respect to the Central grants released upto  financial year 201 -20 
need to be liquidated at the earliest.  The Committee further hopes that the Ministry 
will apprise the current pending UCs involving the total amount and steps taken to 
liquidate the pending UCs.  
(Para 3.20.4) 
DRUG MANUFACTURING INDUSTRY 
 The Committee is of the considered view that vibrant, dynamic strengthened 
drug testing laboratories is concomitant efficient and effective drug regulatory 
mechanism to avert the prevalence of sub -standard drugs, therefore, the Ministry 
should instruct and guide the State Governments to strengthen State Drugs Regulatory 
System.  Moreover, the Committee wants to be informed of the response of State 
Governments of Maharashtra, Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, Tamil Nadu and Karnataka to the 
Ministry’s perusal for submitting the project proposals matching the i ndicative amount 
of each State. U nderstandably the Ministry will continue to monitor optimal utilization 
of fund earmarked for the scheme. 
(Para 3.21.7) 
NATIONAL MENTAL HEALTH PROGRAMME 
 
 The Committee desires to know the status on opening the S ingle Nodel Agency 
Account (SNA) by the Institution for further release of funds under NMHP.  The 
Committee hopes that facilities available under DMHP at CHC and PHC level w ould 
ensure successful exe cution of NMHP in direction of reducing the Mental Health 
burden in the country.  The Committee further wishes to know the fund allocated to 
IEC for awareness generation activities in the school, workplaces and community.  
Besides that the Ministry may apprise the Committee about the measures undertaken to 
reduce the Mental Health burden in the country.  
(Para 3.22.5) 
 
ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW MEDICAL COLLEGES 
 The Committee notes that out of 157 sanctioned medical colleges 72 medical 
colleges have become functional.  The Committee, however, desires to know the status of 
the Letter of Permission submitted by 36 new medical colleges to NMC for commencing 
the courses from academic session 2022 -23.   The Committee further recommends the 
Ministry to incentivize State Government to invite proposal for upgrading the 
educational infrastructure in existing medical colleges so that quality education could be 
imparted in those medical colleges.  The Committee also hopes that the Ministry would

take up the matter of op erationasation of remaining sanctioned medical colleges at the 
earliest.  
(Para 3.23.3) 
MEDICAL EDUCATION STANDARDS AND PROFESSIONAL COMPETENCE 
 The Committee is of the view that in order to ensure medical education standard 
and professional competence in medical colleges, the provision for human resources and 
technical expertise be made at the time of sanctioning of operationalization of medical 
colleges, itself so that quality of education imparted is not compromised. The Committee 
hopes that po sting the status of construction projects alongwith release of fund  on the 
dashboard would strengthen the monitoring mechanism besides making the system 
more transparent, result oriented and avoidance of time and cost overruns.  
(Para 3.24.3) 
 
PRADHAN MANTRI AYUSHM AN BHARAT HEALTH INFRASTRUCTURE 
MISSION (PM-ABHIM) 
 The Committee aspires to know the total actual expenditure incurred on various

execution of PM -ABHIM the health infrast ructure and consolidation of healthcare 
services.

CHAPTER I 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH HAVE BEEN ACCEPTED BY THE 
MINISTRY 
 
1.1  Vision of the Department 
 
Recommendation 
 
1.1.1 The Committee recognizes the vision of the Department of Health Research and 
acknowledges the objectives set by the Department to achieve the set vision. However, the 
Committee is of the strong opinion that with changing times and fickle nature of the health 
emergencies, the Department needs to continuously evaluate its objectives and approach and 
recalibrate it, if the need arises. The Committee also believes that no objective can be achieved 
in its entirety if the Department functions in isolation or in association with research based 
institutes only. The Committee, therefore, recommends that to realize its vision, DHR must 
work in synergy with various departments and Ministries of the Central and State Governments 
as well as the leaders in healthcare industry in the private sector. 
(Para -1.3 of 135th Report) 
 
Action Taken 
 
1.1.2 The Department of Health Research along with ICMR is working in tandem with various 
Departments and Ministries of the Central and State Governments as well as private sector. 
ICMR has launched consortiums in the area of high priority areas like TB, Malaria and  Cancer. 
The aim is to bring together all major national players (with international collaborators) to 
address overarching scientific questions to tackle these health issues in a mission mode.  
 
1.1.3 In battle against COVID -19, ICMR worked in coherence wi th centre and state health 
departments, other S &T agencies and private partners like Bharat Biotech & Zydus Cadilla to 
bring out various solutions ranging from ramping up the testing infrastructure to developing 
diagnostic kit for national serosurveillance to developing a fully indigenous vaccine. 
 
1.1.4 ICMR-DHR-Centre of Excellences (CoE) for fostering MedTechinnovations was 
established at seven IITs viz., IIT -Bombay, IIT -Delhi, IIT -Guwahati, IIT -Hyderabad, IIT -
Kanpur, IIT-Kharagpur and IIT -Madras. These centres of excellence for Medical Device and 
Diagnostic development have been set up with an aim to develop the products/technologies in 
synergy with the requirements of the National Health Mission, Ayushman Bharat and Public 
Health Programs of the Government of India for their potential deployment. 
 
1.1.5 ICMR works in  collaboration with national pro grammes like NV BDCP, NACO etc. to 
generate new evidence to eliminate the communicable diseases like lymphatic filariasis, 
kalazar, AIDS, leprosy etc. As per the recommendation by eminent members of the committee, 
DHR-ICMR will work towards further strengthening the inter -departmental, inter sectoral 
collaborations to bring out logical solutions to health challenges of the nation. 
 
 
 
 

3 
 
1.2  Data and Projection Models 
   
 Recommendation 
 
1.2.1 The Committee recommends Department of Health Research to work with independent 
experts and statistical organizations to ensure that it has the best possible data and projection 
models to inform their thinking. 
(Para 2.12 ibid) 
 
Action Taken  
 
1.2.2 ICMR has a full-fledged institute, National Institute of Medical Statistics (NIMS) that has 
contributed immensely in the area of AIDS, COVID -19 etc. The projections in the demand for 
COVID-19 realted essential supplies for the whole country were also handled under the 
leadership of ICMR-NIMS. ICMR is planning to recruit biostatiscians in mission mode and is 
also working in the capacity building programmes to create a talent pipeline of skilled 
biostatisticians. 
 
1.2.3 As suggested by committee, Department will develop a framework and identify 
independent experts from different statistical organisations to work on data and disease 
modelling. Recently, ICMR collaborated with IITs and Imperial College, Lo ndon to carry out 
modelling in the area of COVID-19. 
 
 
1.3  Ramping up testing capacity 
 
Recommendation 
 
1.3.1 The Committee agrees that India did ramp up its testing capacity exponentially since the 
pandemic began in January 2020. Yet; it's true that as c ompared to several other countries with 
high case load, India's testing numbers remained low under whelming. 
(para 2.24 ibid) 
 
Action Taken 
 
1.3.2 In terms of cumulative numbers, India is second highest in COVID -19 testing in the 
world with more than 86 crore tests done till now. India made sure to optimally use its testing 
capacity as per the requirement through calibrated testing approach. As per WHO guidance a 
140 tests per million population per week were recommended. However, India’s average 
testing remained close to 900 -1000 tests per million population per week. Besides, the total 
testing numbers at the peak of 2 nd and 3rd wave were higher than many developed nations like 
USA and UK. 
 
1.4  Establishment of VRDLs 
 
Recommendation 
 
1.4.1 The Department has submitted that till date 132 VRDLs have been established across 25 
States and 5 Union Territories. These Viral Research and Diagnostic Laboratories (VRDLs) 

4 
 
are established in a three -tier mode, viz., Regional, State and Medical College L evel. Regional 
level VRDLs are equipped with serology, RT-PCR, virus isolation, sequencing and fluorescence 
microscopy; State Level labs are equipped with serology, RT - PCR, fluorescence microscopy 
and sequencing, while Medical College Level are equipped w ith serology and Rt -PCR. These 
VRDLs are intended to cover the entire country for timely diagnosis/identification of viruses 
during outbreaks of epidemics, generation of data about viral diseases for facilitating quick 
deployment of adequate resources and measures to save the human lives during outbreaks. 
(Para 3.2 ibid) 
 
Action Taken 
 
1.4.2 As on April 2022, a total of 136 VRDLs have been setup across the country spread over 
25 States and 5 UTs. The VRDL network is a three tiered system comprising of regio nal level, 
state level and medical college level laboratories designated as top level, middle level and 
lower level respectively. During the subsequent expansion of the VRDL network, equal 
geographic coverage of the country has been ensured.  
 
1.4.3 The VRDLs are equipped with state -of-art laboratory infrastructure, capable to diagnose 
more than 25 viruses of public health importance. Further impetus has been given to strengthen 
the VRDL network by implementing coordinated research activities on advance dia gnosis, 
robust surveillance mechanism for various virus diseases, epidemiological studies, outbreaks 
detections etc. 
 
1.4.4 Each laboratory has linkage with local health authorities and are being supplied field 
samples of any outbreak cluster with the help  IDSP and their sentinel sites. The data with 
respect to outbreak investigations and diagnosis is being uploaded on real -time basis to the 
dedicated data mining center operational at ICMR -NIE, Chennai. The interpretation/analysis of 
the data is parallel reported to the respective health authorities at Central and State level.   
 
1.5 Establishment of 3 tier VRDLs 
 
Recommendation 
 
1.5.1 The Committee observes that since Viral Research and Diagnostic Laboratories  (VRDLs) 
are established in a three -tier mode, viz., Regional, State and Medical College Level. VRDLs 
can be established in Sikkim and Nagaland as well at regional and state level even if there is no 
Medical College in these two States. The Committee notes that the States of Sikkim and 
Nagaland had highest fatality rate among st all the North -Eastern States.  Non-availability of 
testing facility could have been one of the reasons for high causality. The Committee, therefore, 
recommends DHR to work in associati on with the State Governments of North -Eastern Region 
and establish VRDLs in any government run research centre or any government hospital. 
(Para 3.4 ibid) 
 
Action Taken 
 
1.5.2 As per the scheme norms, VRDLs can be establish in government medical 
colleges/research institutions/army hospitals. Due to unavailability of medical colleges in the 
State of Sikkim and Nagaland, the VRDLs could not be setup. However, DHR will explore the 
potential sites in the mentioned States.  

5 
 
 
1.5.3 Besides that, a viral diagnostic laboratory is functional at STNM Hospital, Gangtok, 
Sikkim since 2015 with financial support from ICMR. The said lab is equipped with all 
necessary infrastructures and trained human resources. The lab is catering whole Sikk im region 
efficiently. 
 
1.6  Establishment of MRHRU 
 
 Recommendation 
 
1.6.1 The Committee, therefore recommends DHR to work assiduously in establishing MRHRU 
in each state and UT of the country considering the poor state of health technology in almost 
all Indian States. The Committee also recommends the Department to approve and establish 
more such units in the rural part of country and accordingly the Department must seek 
adequate funds for the scheme at the RE stage and in subsequent years. 
(Para 3.27 ibid) 
 
Action Taken  
 
1.6.2 The Department also has the target of establishing 01 MRHRU in each State and Union 
Territory. Accordingly, the recommendation of the Committee has been noted for guidance and 
compliance. 
 
 1.7  Capacity Building and Skill Development 
 
Recommendation 
 
1.7.1 The Committee takes note of the efforts put by DHR for capacity building and skill 
development of the human resource. However, the Committee believes that the major problem 
now-a-days in medical research is its sub -standard quality. Poor quality medical research 
leads to almost no or little impact in clinical practice. The Committee takes note that in India, 
faculties and scientists in medical institutions, are largely engaged in teaching and clinical 
care and there is very little number of scientists interested in medical research. 
(Para 3.37 ibid) 
 
Action Taken 
 
1.7.2 In order to promote quality research, the subject specific calls with well -defined research 
questions have been initiated upon brainstorming discussions with the biomedical experts. 
 
1.8  Quality of Medical Research 
 
Recommendation 
 
1.8.1 The Committee is of the strong view that quality of medical research can only be 
improved by inviting large no. of scientists, who can devote specific time for research f rom 
medical institutions especially in the field of diseases engulfing the country. The Committee, 
therefore, recommends utilizing college facilities having specific and exclusive time for 
research activities. The Committee also recommends that there shoul d be added incentives for 

6 
 
researchers for conducting high-quality and viable medical research that can be translated into 
action in treatment of life threatening diseases. 
(Para 3.38 ibid) 
 
Action Taken 
 
1.8.2 The observation of the Hon’ble Committee is no ted and will work towards implementing 
them.  
 
1.9  Basic Objective of HTAIn 
 
 Recommendation 
 
1.9.1 The Committee acknowledges the basic objective of HTAIn i.e. to analyse the health 
technologies viz. medicines, devices and health programmes  for its cost- effectiveness, clinical-
effectiveness and equity issues by means of Health Technology Assessment (HTA), and in turn 
helping in decision making for an optimal utilization of allocated health budget. The Committee 
believes that HTAIn scheme an d the scheme of establishing Model Rural Health Research 
Units (MRHRU), if operated in consonance & conjunction to each other can greatly aid in 
improving the overall health infrastructure, particularly in rural and semi -urban areas. The 
Committee, believes that adequate budgetary allocation and subsequent optimal utilization of 
allocated funds under this scheme would also help in minimizing the cost for healthcare by 
reducing the out of pocket expenditure that still remains enormous. The Committee notes th at 
out of the 17 Resource Centres of HTAIn only one such centre is in NE region and none in the 
UT of J&K and Ladakh. The Committee, therefore, recommends DHR to work towards setting 
up at least one such centre in J&K/Ladakh and one more in NE region. 
(Para 3.44 ibid) 
 
Action Taken 
 
1.9.2 Resource Centre is available at Indian Institute of Public Health (IIPH), Shillong in NE 
Region. However, the recommendation of the Hon’ble Committee to constitute a centre in UT 
of Jammu &Kashmir and Ladakh will be consid ered and the recommendation of the Hon’ble 
Committee regarding HTAIn and MRHRU schemes working in conjunction and consonance 
with each other for improving the overall health infrastructure has been noted for compliance. 
 
1.10  Specialized Cancer Centre in NER 
 
Recommendation 
 
1.10.1 The Committee understands that North -Eastern states have the highest incidence of 
Cancer in India, for example Mizoram has the highest incidence of stomach cancer, Meghalaya 
has big number of esophageal cancer cases and Nagaland reports high Nasopharyngeal cancer 
cases, but due to unavailability of specialized facilities, patients often visit other cities of India 
for diagnosis and treatment. Thus, specialized cancer centre for screening, early diagnosis and 
treatment of cancer within the region needs to be  established. The Committee, therefore, 
recommends DHR to fast track setting up of oncopathology labs in NE region. 
(Para 3.47 ibid) 
 

7 
 
Action Taken 
 
1.10.2 The DHR ICMR advanced Molecular oncopathology diagnostic services have been set 
up in Cachar Cancer I nstitute in Silchur and RIMS, Imphal. The suggestion of the Hon’ble 
Committee regarding Mizoram will also be considered as and when a proposal is received from 
Mizoram. 
 
1.11  Allocation of Fund to ICMR 
  
Recommendation 
 
1.11.1 Considering the pivotal role of Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR) in the field 
of bio -medical and health research in India, the Committee is deeply concerned to note the 
large gap in funding of ICMR when compared with health research institutions of countries like 
US, UK, France and China. What worries the Committee more is that the allocation of fund to 
ICMR and subsequent utilization of funds by ICMR has always been less than the projected 
demand, even in the Covid -years, where the need for adequa te funds and optimal utilization 
was call of the hour. The Committee believes that the budgetary allocation to ICMR in 2022 -
23, is grossly inadequate keeping in view the mandate of the ICMR. However, the Committee is 
also aware that the utilization trends of ICMR over the years don‟t present a justified reason 
for increase of funds. The Committee, therefore, recommends ICMR to improve the absorption 
capacity of its scheme implementing agencies. The Committee recommends ICMR to provide 
more money for researc h projects, joint -research projects with national and international 
bodies, establish net work of labs for diagnosis of Communicable and Non - Communicable 
diseases, extensively fund research projects, provide trainings/ international exposure to 
researchers, develop programmes to encourage youth to take up research, scheme to develop 
inclination towards health-research in students of higher-secondary and senior secondary. 
(Para 4.5 ibid) 
 
Action Taken  
 
1.11.2 The observation of the Hon’ble Committee is noted. Some more centers under ICMR like 
Center at Nagpur, Jabalpur, Chandigarh, Bangalore & Dibrugarh are under Construction. These 
Centers will cater the enhanced need of the Country and will also increase the absorption 
capacity of ICMR. 
 
1.12  Dual-Use Research 
 
Recommendation 
 
1.12.1 The Committee, therefore, recommends DHR -ICMR to formulate regulations and 
national policy for oversight of dual -use research - which refers to experiments that are 
conducted for peaceful purposes but can be modified or altered to cause harm. The Committee 
further recommends DHR/ICMR to conduct trainings and develop strict and exhaustive 
guidelines on bio-safety and bio-security. 
(Para 4.11 ibid) 
 
 
 

8 
 
Action Taken 
 
1.12.2 DHR-ICMR conducts regular training in the area of bio safety & Bio security including 
BSL-3 and GLP. ICMR/DHR has also notified a BSL -3 certification committee for regularly 
monitoring the facility design, operationalization, projects undertaken and pathog ens stored. 
Also a high level BSL -4 expert committee has been notified and is operational now. ICMR has 
also developed exhaustive guidelines on biosafety and biosecurity which have been disseminated 
to all eligible laboratories. As guided, ICMR will work towards developing a robust plan. 
 
1.13  Lack of public confidence in Healthcare 
 
Recommendation 
 
1.13.1 The Committee, however, believes that there is a general lack of public confidence in 
healthcare/pharmaceutical industry and the Committee apprehends t hat slackening public 
confidence might pose a hurdle in conducting clinical trials. The Committee recommends 
ICMR to work in cohesion with the pharmaceutical industry to regain trust of the general 
public by engaging more transparently. The ICMR should als o make more efforts to educate 
and inform patients and the society at large about the benefits of engaging in clinical research 
and allowing authentic collection of patient data. 
(Para 4.15 ibid) 
 
Action Taken 
 
1.13.2 The Communications Unit of ICMR is working continuously to bring mass awareness 
regarding the procedure of drug/vaccine development and also tackle the vaccine hesitancy 
among the population. As  guided by the committee ICMR would develop a program to educ ate 
and inform patients and society about the benefits of engaging in clinical research. 
 
1.14  Projects taken by ICMR 
 
Recommendation  
 
1.14.1 The Committee takes note of the projects under taken by ICMR along with different 
organizations of the Ayush . The Committee is of the view that Ayurveda, Homeopathy, Siddha, 
Unani and herbal medicines have wide socio cultural acceptance with large chunk of 
population subscribing to the alternative mode of treatment, but the Committee believes that 
scientific research is needed, so that these regimens can be incorporated as standard treatment 
regimens. Research on Ayush preparations must be conducted scientifically so that it is in line 
with the modern patenting system. The Committee, therefore, recommends ICMR to  work 
towards linking various disciplines of Ayush with each other and also with modern system of 
medicine, as it may lead to a possible convergence of various disciplines for global benefit. 
(Para 4.17 ibid) 
 
Action Taken 
 
1.14.2 ICMR through its institut e ICMR -National Institute of Traditional Medicine (ICMR -
NITM) has envisioned to influence public health outcomes by integrating Traditional Medicine 
(TM) with Modern Health System, through Research, Human Resource Development and 
 

9 
 
Outreach. ICMR -NITM is wor king on developing evidence -based, affordable, traditional 
medicine solutions for public health concerns, which may be further integrated with modern 
healthcare systems. More than 1500 TM formulations from 750 TM practitioners involving 
1200 species of pla nts has been documented.  The scientific evidences are being created 
through (i) Pharmaco -epidemiological studies on utility of TM practices (ii) Robust 
observational studies (iii) Pre-clinical evaluations through in silico, in vitro and in vivo studies 
of the selected practices (iv) Clinical evaluation of the selected preparations/ practices that 
include Model Rural Health Research Units as rural sites (v) Implementation research & 
development of policies and recommendations on models of integration. ICMR -NITM created 
a database on ethnomedicinal plants of Western Ghats (http://nitmmedplantsdb.in), successfully 
validated the TM practice for osteoarthritis, filed provisional patent on TM formulation for 
COVID-19.  ICMR -NITM aims to provide an interface of Mo dern Healthcare System and 
Traditional Healthcare System by recommending use of validated traditional medicine, training 
to create a cadre of integrative health care researchers and professionals and human resource 
development and developing policies and g uidelines. Thus, its activities are not limited to 
drug/product development but to ensure integration of already validated traditional medicine, 
skill-sets and knowledge-base to the existing healthcare system. 
 
1.15  Funding Health Research Institutions 
 
Recommendation 
 
1.15.1 Analysing the data from the 2016 evaluation the Committee observes that, there is wide 
gap in funding between health research institutions of countries like US, UK, Australia, China 
and Brazil and ICMR. The Committee further observes  that though annual output (in terms of 
paper published) of ICMR has continued to grow with respect to its 2005 output and in2014, 
ICMR produced 108% more papers than it did in 2005, however, the Committee believes that 
this won't be a just comparison with  NIH (National Institute of Health, US) as NIH is already 
working at a very high output, and given a larger base, it's rate of growth (in terms of paper 
published) cannot be as high as ICMR. The Committee further notes that just the number of 
paper published cannot be a sufficient indicator for performance, as the quality of research, its 
significance in public health and its viability are far more important factors in performance 
analysis. 
(Para 4.20 ibid) 
 
Action Taken 
 
1.15.2 ICMR agrees with the Committ ee’s observation that numbers of publication are not 
sufficient indicator for performance. To further elaborate on ICMR’s activities and 
achievements in public health, it has contributed to the development of several diagnostic 
solutions to health challeng es including COVID -19, Nipah, TB, Haemoglonopathies, KFD, 
Chandipura Virus etc. It has also been involved in development of life - saving vaccines against

2.11  Establishment of BSL-IV and BSL-III Labs 
 
Recommendation 
 
2.11.1 The Committee notes the establishment of 2 new BSL-IV and three new BSL-III labs. The

understands that the two new BSL -IV labs would co ver the East and West part of India, 

16 
 
however, the North and South India still don‟t have BSL -IV labs. The Committee believes that 
in the absence of well -equipped and high -tech labs, samples have to be transported over long 
distances to the nearest lab. this causes delay in diagnosis often leading to serious 
repercussions over result of diagnostic test. The Committee is of the strong opinion that lack of 
adequate number of BSL -3 and BSL -4 labs would greatly hinder India's chances of defeating 
viral outbre aks thereby exposing India's large population to various deadly diseases. The 
Committee, therefore, recommends ICMR to establish one BSL-IV lab in each of the four zones. 
The Committee also recommends DHR to launch more mobile laboratories as such mobile 
units could be of great help during outbreaks particularly in rural and remote areas. 
(Para 4.9 ibid) 
 
2.11.2 The Committee is also well aware of the fact that research in BSL -IV labs has its own 
share of fall outs as these facilities are built for research ers to work with the most dangerous 
pathogens. However, the Committee believes that science can enable humanity to reap the 
benefits of research if it meets ethical, considerate and smart policymaking. 
(Para 4.10 ibid) 
 
Action Taken  
 
2.11.3 Operationalization and maintenance of BSL -4 labs is highly demanding and complex. 
Besides, BSL-4 is not needed routinely for outbreak investigation. BSL -4 labs are required for 
animal experiments, growing viruses and undertaking animal challenge studies. These 
specialized research functions are undertaken in BSL -4 as the inoculums of the pathogen 
generated for these experiments is very high, thus increasing vulnerability of the laboratory 
workers to become infected. Besides, the high risk viruses stored in these labs nee d to be 
maintained with utmost caution as any leakage from these labs can lead to havoc in the country. 
Constructing too many BSL -4s is not advisable due to biological threats. The BSL -3 labs are 
more than adequate for handling high risk pathogens and unde rtaking investigation of 
pandemics/epidemics. As of now, there are 18 BSL -3 labs operational/ under construction 
within the ICMR/DHR network. Also ICMR/DHR has developed a mobile BSL-3 lab in public 
private partnership. This lab is operational and will take pandemic preparedness to next level as 
it can be driven to the outbreak site and made operational within 24-48 hours.

3.1  Rapid Response Teams (RRT) 
 
Recommendation 
 
3.1.1  The Committee recommends DHR - ICMR to establish and manage Rapid Response 
Teams (RRT)  consisting of epidemiologists, immunologists, virologists, experts of infectious 
disease, physicians and other relevant scientific and clinical staff to counter any emergency 
situations developing due to disease Outbreaks. 
(Para1.4 ibid) 
 
Action Taken 
 
3.1.2 During COVID-19, ICMR convened National Task Force (NTF) consisting of eminent 
epidemiologists, public health experts, physicians, virologists & other clinical scientists to 
deliberate on various aspects of disease outbreak including Diagnostics, Epi demiology & 
Surveillance, Operational Research (OR) & Clinical Research.  
 
3.1.3  At present, a multidisciplinary team of epidemiologists, virologist and immunologists 
does exist in ICMR Institutes, involved in outbreak investigation. Besides, each Institute of

Further Recommendation 
 
3.1.4  The Committee appreciates the existence of the multi -disciplinary team consisting 
of epidemiologists, virologists and immunologists at ICMR. The Committee, however, 
intends to convey the Government that the Rapid Response Team (RRT) must be at the 
alert mode to meet any eventualities of Biological and Chemical weapons/warfare, besides 
combating the challenges posed by the outbreak of endemic or pandemic. Such oversight 
body should not only have relevant linkages with clinical operational and clinical research 
institutes but also integrated co -ordination with national decision making body viz., NITI 
Aayog, PMO and Cabinet Secretariat to ward off or keep vigil against any possible 
biological or chemical warfare so that appropriate decision is taken with out delay even of 
an hour. The Committee understands that the Government needs to incorporate the 
component of biological/chemical, deterrence in its national security strategy.

3.4  Emergency Epidemic Preparedness and Response 
 
Recommendation 
 
3.4.1 The Committee observes that in 2020 -21, out of the Rs. 1,275.00 crores released to 
ICMR, actual expenditure was only 1,236.30 crores. Similarly, in 2021-22 out of the total funds 
allocation of Rs. 526.28 crores the ICMR spent Rs. 232.72 crores only. The Co mmittee 
expresses its serious concern over partial utilisation of fund allocated under Emergency 
Epidemic Preparedness and Response. The Committee does not agree with the Department's 
version that less utilization of the allocated funds, did not affect in any way the physical 
achievements both in terms of procurement of testing kits, setting up of testing labs and 
creating the testing capacity in the country. Contrary to Department's reflection, the deadly 
second wave overwhelmed India's Covid -19 testing in frastructure. The second wave scores of 
people with symptoms of the disease could not get themselves tested, since labs were fully 
booked and test reports were significantly delayed. In many places, this delay in delivery of 
reports meant that seriously il l patients in dire need of comprehensive treatment couldn't get 
hospitalized and as a result scores of people died too. 
(Para 2.23 ibid) 
 
Action Taken 
 
3.4.2  ICMR has prepared the budget for Covid -19 during the F.Y. 2020 –21 on the basis of 
anticipated requirement for the Covid -19 testing kits for all over India with the anticipated 
prices as on May – June 2020. However, Government has decided in September 2020 that  
States will procure the kits themselves which resulted less number of procurement by ICMR.     
The rates of kits have been also reduced too much as compared to March – April 2020 to post 
September 2020. During the second wave of infections, some labs where the case load was high, 
had an exceeded in-turnaround time (> 48 – 72 hours) in a proportion of cases due to very high 
demand for testing. 
 
3.4.3 Besides, many States and Offices (Private & Government Organizations) imposed a 
demand for testing of even healthy individuals, during inter-state travel or attending Office. This 
was not as per the National Covid -19 Guidelines of ICMR and Ministry of Health & Family 
Welfare and this resulted in overwhelming of labs un-necessarily. 
 
Further Recommendation  
 
3.4.4 The Committee is not in agreement with DHR’s plea of partial utilization of fund 
allocated under Emergency Epidemic Preparedness and Response. The delayed delivery of 
investigation reports & long waiting in queue of patients at hospital corridors & gates 
resulting into more than 5 lakh death during Second Wave of Pandemic Covid -19 are 
testimony to the fact of exhibiting mismanagement of Pandemic Covid-19. All Government 

20 
 
machinery reached to the point of grinding halt. The Committee understands the 
limitation of DHR over its anticipating capacity in the situation of unpredicted and 
unprecedented global health emergencies. However, the Committee recommends ICMR to 
enhance its professional pursuit and operational efficiency to meet any future health 
eventualities of this magnitude or more than this . The Committee further recommends 
ICMR to undertake project to make in -depth research/studies to predict/pre -hand 
revelation of possible outbreak of Pandemic by adopting the sewage sample test etc.

3.6  Viral Research and Diagnostic Laboratories (VRDLs) 
 
Recommendation 
 
3.6.1 The Committee is pleased to note that the scheme for establishing Viral Research and

3.6.4 The DHR/ICMR is doing handholding of the VRDLs with the help of resource centers

systems, sampling & transportation to further reduce the turnaround time from 24-48 hours. 
 
Further Recommendation 
 
3.6.5 The Committee, notes that the DHR/ICMR is doing handholding of the VRDLs with 
the help of resource centers (NIV -Pune & NIE Chennai) by providing trainings on

3.7.3 The Committee gives impetus to the need of a network of quality testing 
infrastructure in the country to map the various health index of the whole population to 
the extent of last miles of the country. The committee, therefore,  recommends DHR to 
expand the scope of VRDL scheme to cover the remote rural and tribal areas of the 
country. The Committee further recommends the Ministry of Finance to allocate higher 
allocation to the said scheme and extend its period of time years for implementation till 
achievement of its ideal objective of setting up of one VRDL in each district. 
 
 3.8  Establishment of MRUs 
 
Recommendation 
 
3.8.1 The Committee has been given to understand that so far, 92 MRUs are approved in the 
country and the Department's target was to set up 6 MRUs in 2021 -22. The Committee 
observes that like in 2021 -22, the MRU scheme has been allocated Rs. 60 crores only for t he 
same target of setting up 6 MRUs in 2022 -23. The Committee recommends DHR to set higher 
targets every year and seek more allocation for the scheme to increase the spread/network of 
MRUs in the country as there are no MRU in several states and the States  like Bihar and 
Chhattisgarh don‟t have MRUs in commensurate to the population of States. 
(Para 3.19 ibid) 
 
Action Taken 
 
3.8.2 Targets for setting up new MRUs in a year are decided on the basis of past trends, 
requirements and availability of funds. All t he States and Union Territories are addressed 
regularly to send proposals for setting up of MRUs in Medical Colleges.  The MRU scheme 
approved for 2021-22 to 2025-26 envisages establishing of 30 MRUs, i.e. 06 MRUs every year. 
However, against the target of  establishing 06 MRUs in 2021 -22, 11 MRUs were actually 
approved. 
 
Further Recommendation 
 
3.8.3 The Committee reiterates its recommendation to DHR to seek allocation for the 
scheme to increase the spread/network of MRUs in the country as there are no MRU in 
several states and the States like Bihar and Chhattisgarh don’t have MRUs in 
commensurate to the population of States. 
 
 
3.9  Setting up MRUs in NER 
 
Recommendation 
 
3.9.1 The Committee has observed that no MRU has been established in Sikkim, Nagaland, 
Meghalaya and Arunachal Pradesh. Given the increasing Cancer cases in north-eastern States, 
the Committee is of the considered view that the Department must work in tandem wit h the 
respective State Governments and set up MRUs in these States at the earliest. The Committee 
believes that good clinical research infrastructure at the local level in the State can help boost 

23 
 
country's fight against Cancer and severe non - communicable diseases like Hypertensions and 
cardio-vascular diseases. 
(Para 3.20 ibid) 
 
Action Taken 
 
3.9.2 MRUs in Govt. Medical colleges are established on the basis of proposals received from 
State Governments.  MRUs in the State of Arunachal Pradesh, Assam, Mizoram and Nagaland 
have been established under the MRU scheme of ICMR. Now, these have been taken over by 
DHR. 
 
Further Recommendation 
 
3.9.3 Keeping in view the geographical landscape of NER, the Committee recommends for 
intensive network of MRU for ens uring basic infrastructure of clinical investigation and 
research work for region specific study of Biology of Diseases. The Committee is of the 
considered view that only better research infrastructure would provide adequate facilities 
for treatment of can cer and other life threatening communicable and non -communicable 
diseases viz. Hypertension and cardio -vascular disease. The Committee, therefore, 
reiterates its recommendation for setting up of MRUs in Sikkim and Meghalaya.  
 
3.10  Operationalisation of MRUs 
 
Recommendation 
 
3.10.1 The Committee also observes that though 92 MRUs are approved in the country but all 
the MRUs are not functional, the Committee finds no point in just announcing and approving 
MRUs if there is not enough manpower and infrastructure at the ground level. The Committee, 
therefore, recommends Department to reduce the delay between the dates of the announcement 
of approval and the actual operationalisation of MRUs at the ground level. 
(Para 3.21ibid) 
 
Action Taken 
 
3.10.2 The Time lag between the initial sanction of an MRU and the subsequent 
operationalization of that MRU is generally due to the time taken in awarding contracts for 
Civil Works and procurement of equipment and the recruitment of staff.  These functions in 
State Govt. Medical Colleges are regulated by the rules/instructions of the respective State 
Governments.  Process in these activities is, however, monitored regularly through periodical 
progress reports and virtual review meetings. The recommendation of the  Parliamentary 
Committee has, however, been noted for guidance and compliance. 
 
Further Recommendation 
 
3.10.3 The Committee feels that DHR should take concrete steps for reducing the time lag 
between sanctioning of an MRU and operationalization of MRU uni t. The Committee 
does not approve the procedural delay in awarding civil works and procurement of 
equipment. The DHR, therefore, should have effective supervision and monitoring over 
the progress of the MRU projects. To avoid the delay, the Committee recom mends DHR 

24 
 
to get the technical and human resource strength sanctioned at the time of sanctioning of 
the project, itself.  
 
3.11  Objective of the MRHRU Scheme 
 
Recommendation 
 
3.11.1 The Committee notes that the objective of the MRHRU scheme is to transfer  modern 
technology for tackling the disease burden in rural India. The Committee is of the view that 
considering the havoc caused by Covid-19, particularly the second wave of Covid-19, there is a 
dire need to beef up health infrastructure in the rural India. The modern healthcare equipments 
and technologies which are generally limited to urban centres should be taken to the rural 
healthcare facilities as well. The Committee observes that despite the year -on-year increase in 
the budget of the scheme, the tar get to set up MRHRUs is decreasing from 7 in 2019 -20 to 2 in 
2021-22. For 2022 -23 also the target is to set up 2 MRHRUs only. The Committee further 
observes that there is no MRHRU in the vast state like Uttar Pradesh and also the UT of 
Ladakh. 
(Para 3.26 ibid) 
 
Action Taken 
 
3.11.2 The targets are decided on the basis of past trends, proposals received from State 
Governments and available resources.  State Governments, ICMR, Directors of ICMR 
Institutes are regularly addressed to send their proposals. 
 
Further Recommendation 
 
3.11.3 The Committee recommends DHR for taking pro -active steps in incentivizing the 
State Government to prepare proposal on setting up of MRHRU in rural areas. Extensive 
and equitable distribution of MRHRU would ensure the facility  of understanding Biology 
of various diseases in tribal and remote rural areas and thus ensure access to affordable 
treatment. The DHR, therefore, need to work in tandem with State Government and seek 
enhanced budgetary allocation from the Ministry of Fina nce for laying out network of 
MRHRU for ensuring availability of Modern tools, methods, equipments and technologies 
in rural healthcare system.  
 
 
3.12  Proposal for fellowship/training 
 
Recommendation 
 
3.12.1 The Committee observes that over the past three years the reason for under - utilisation 
of the allocated funds has been same i.e. due to receipt of less number of proposal for 
fellowship/training. The Committee understands that unless there is adequate bud getary 
allocation followed by optimal utilization of allocated fund, the objective to create a large pool 
of trained and skilled medical researchers would not be realized. The Committee is not 
satisfied with Department repeating the same reason for less nu mber of proposals for 
fellowship/training for under-utilisation of the allocated funds. The Committee desires to know 
the concrete steps taken by DHR to increase the number of proposals for fellowship/training. 

25 
 
The Committee strongly feels that there is no  dearth of talent in our country, hence the DHR 
should work on establishing institutional mechanism to attract scientists for submitting more 
proposals for fellowship under the schemes of DHR. 
(Para 3.33 ibid) 
 
3.12.2 The Committee observes that over the past 9 years, DHR's efforts to encourage Indian 
health research personnel serving abroad and coming back to India has paid little dividends as 
in these 9 years only 10 persons have availed this offer. The Committee ther efore, recommends 
that the Department must analyse the programme and find out the reasons as to why the scheme 
has few takers. The Committee also recommends that DHR must develop a conducive 
environment and offer lucrative prospects to Indian researches se rving abroad, so that they are 
encouraged to come back to their country of birth and serve their country. 
 
(Para 3.34) 
 
Action Taken 
 
3.12.3 Following initiatives have been taken by the DHR in order to attract scientists for 
submitting more proposals with better research quality: 
 
1. For wider publicity the scheme was advertised in the national daily newspapers 
and social media platforms. 
 
2. Monthly stipend and research grant has been enhanced. 
 
3. Evaluation of the proposals, for those projects which are weak and require 
modification, the experts committee members provide the guidance and 
opportunity to modify the proposals. 
 
Further Recommendation 
 
3.12.4  The Committee considers the need for creation of poo l of trained and skilled 
medical researchers in various fields to eliminate/eradicate various diseases in the country 
through in depth study, understanding Biology of Disease and find out solution for 
eradication in a time -bound manner. The Committee, ther efore, emphasizes the need for 
establishing institutional mechanism and simplification of procedures for inviting larger 
number of proposals for fellowship under the scheme governed by DHR. 
 
 
3.13  Human Resource Development for Health Research 
 
Recommendation 
 
3.13.1 The Committee observes that over the years there has been gross underutilization of the 
funds allocated and like in the case of Human Resource Development for Health Research 
component, the reason for under-utilization is same for all the years. The Committee notes that 
during last three years i.e. 2019-20, 2020-21 and 2021-22, RE allocation has significantly been 
reduced, thereby implying that DHR did not get enough viable research projects to be 
undertaken and appropriation of alloc ated fund thereon. The Committee recommends DHR to 

26 
 
make serious efforts to identify research projects which have potential for treatment of diseases 
and therefore rational utilisation of allocated funds could be made. The Committee, strongly 
suggests DHR t o promote research and encourage researchers to undertake research for the 
benefit of public health. The Committee also recommends that in view of the increasing 
biological threats, the DHR should put more emphasis on research related to biological 
weapons to ensure that in the eventuality of biological attacks, the country is safeguarded 
against any biological warfare. 
(Para 3.41 ibid) 
 
Action Taken 
 
3.13.2 The observation of the Hon’ble  Committee is noted and efforts will be made to identify 
research projects having potential for treatment of diseases and utilization of allocated funds. 
Following initiatives have been taken by the DHR in order to attract scientists for submitting 
more proposals with better research quality: 
 
1. For wider publicity the scheme was advertised in the national daily newspapers and social 
media platforms. 
 
2. Evaluations of the proposals, for those projects which are weak and require modification, 
the experts  committee members provide the guidance and opportunity to modify the 
proposals. 
 
Further Recommendation 
 
3.13.3 The Committee reiterates its recommendation that DHR should encourage and 
emphasize on research relating to surveillance over biological weapon s and chemical 
warfare which have been equally threatening as nuclear weapons. The Committee, cautions 
the Government for chalking out counter strategy to guard the country against possible 
Biological and Chemical attack and therefore, feel the need and ur gency of strengthening 
defence mechanism from the point of Biological and Chemical Weapons.  
  

27 
 
CHAPTER–IV 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS IN RESPECT OF WHICH FINAL REPLIES 
OF THE MINISTRY HAVE NOT BEEN RECEIVED 
4.1  Need for more skilled manpower in future 
 
Recommendation 
 
4.1.1 The Committee is contended to note that the Department is well aware of the need for 
more skilled manpower in future and bringing in more professionalism in its working for 
realizing the objectives of bio-safety and bio-security as well as to deal with diseases identified 
for elimination like TB, Malaria, Filariasis within a definite timeframe. However, the 
Committee, feels that Department should take action to fill the posts of scientific professionals 
so that crucial research work is  not delayed. The Committee recommends Department to fast -
track recruitment processes of skilled and scientific professionals. The Committee further 
recommends DHR to create a work culture and environment which attracts highly skilled 
professional shaving great scientific acumen. The Committee believes that offering lucrative 
career prospects along with a good work -life balance and liberty to carry out world class 
research would definitely attract best scientific brains to ICMR. 
(Para 1.11 ibid) 
Action Taken  
 
4.1.2 As on date, the total sanctioned strength of regular Government employees in the 
Department is 42 out of which 06 sanctioned posts are for Scientist C, D and E. These posts are 
to be filled on Deputation (ISTC) basis. The recruitment p rocess of Scientist C, D & E (02 
posts each) is at advanced stage in consultation with Union Public Service Commission 
(UPSC). 
 
4.1.3 DHR is concerned about intake of trained manpower and has been advertising and 
recruiting scientific positions in mission mode. In last 2 -3 years more than 100 scientists have 
been recruited in ICMR. Recently, scientists posts in the area of Entomology, An imal Resource 
Facility & Hemoglobinopathies Centre. Regular training is imparting in the area of Bioethics & 
Biosafety and Biosecurity. These activities will be strengthened further. 
 
 
4.2  Adequate Funds to Health Research 
 
Recommendation 
 
4.2.1 The Committee observes that for DHR, BE 2021 -22 allocation was Rs. 2663.00 crores 
which was increased to Rs. 3080.00 crores in RE 2021 -22 and the allocation for BE 2022-23 is 
Rs. 3200.65 crores only. The Committee further notes that while the increase in b udget from 
BE 2021-22 to RE 2021-22 is almost 16%, the increase from RE2021 -22 to BE 2022-23 is just 
3.92% only. The Committee further observes that while countries like UK and USA are 
allocating budget of around 2% of their GDP to health research, India w hich faces humongous 
burden of diseases which lead to poverty inducing out -of-pocket health expenditure by its 
population, allocates only 0.02% of its GDP for health research. 
(Para 2.6 ibid) 

28 
 
 
Action Taken 
 
4.2.2  The observation of the Hon’ble Committee is noted. 
 
4.3  Higher Budgetary allocation for Health Research 
 
Recommendation 
 
4.3.1 The Committee is of the view that the increase in health research budget, year on year is 
very meager and is not commensurate with the tasks DHR -ICMR are entr usted to deal with. 
Thus the allocated budget is grossly insufficient to meet the existing and future healthcare 
challenges. The Committee feels that higher budgetary allocation for health research will 
result in more research based findings which in turn would help in devising more informed 
affordable and practical plans/methodologies for diagnosis and treatment of both 
communicable and non -communicable diseases. Higher allocation for health research would 
also make the country better prepared for tackling  any future outbreaks and health exigencies. 
The Committee, in its 127 th Report on Demand for Grants had recommended Government to 
allocate 5 percent of the budget of the Department of Health & Family Welfare to DHR. The 
Committee further reiterates its recommendation to allocate 5% of the total health budget for 
health research in the next two years. The Committee also recommends that considering global 
standards with respect to investment in health research, the Government must invest at least 
0.1% of the GDP in the next five years. Here the Committee also advances its support to DHR 
for seeking higher budgetary allocation from Ministry of Finance. 
(Para 2.7 ibid) 
 
Action Taken 
 
4.3.2 The observation of the Hon’ble Committee is noted. The matter will be pursed with 
Ministry of Finance based on requirements during the RE stage. 
 
4.4  Boosting the absorption capacity of the implementing agencies 
 
Recommendation 
 
4.4.1 The Committee is pleased to observe that the percentage of shortfall/variation as 
compared to "Projected demand" is decreasing year -on-year. Therefore, the Committee is 
hopeful that the Department will continue to improve its fiscal performance by projecti ng 
realistic estimate each year to the Ministry of Finance. However, the Committee feels that that 
on the one hand the Secretary DHR demands 5% of total health budget for health research, on 
the other hand the Department's Projected Demand is nowhere close  to 5% of total health 
budget (Rs. 83,000 crores in BE 2022 - 23). The Committee, therefore, strongly recommends 
that DHR must work towards boosting the absorption capacity of the implementing agencies 
which are tasked with running its schemes across different regions of the country. 
 (Para 2.9 ibid) 
 
 
 
 

29 
 
 
Action Taken  
 
4.4.2 Department is working closely with the implementing agencies by providing training and 
hand holding to improve the quality of proposals received. Along with media advertisement for 
increasing awareness about the schemes. These efforts will ensue boosting in the absorption 
capacity of the implementing agencies and recently, PM-ABHIM schemes has been approved for 
next 5 years covering new activities / centers which are going to start w ithin the ambit of this 
Scheme which will boost the absorption capacity of ICMR. 
 
4.5  Enhance funds absorption capacities 
 
Recommendation 
 
4.5.1 The Committee, over the years, has recommended higher allocation to DHR, including 
for financial year 2022-23. After observing continuous under-utilisation of allocated funds, the 
Committee is of the opinion that seeking higher allocation by the department is not justified 
until the Department and its sister organizations and scheme implementing agencies don‟t 
enhance their funds absorption capacities. The Committee, therefore, urges DHR to boost fund 
absorption capacity of the implementing agencies and all organizations associated with it. The 
Committee also recommends that higher budgetary allocation would be jus tified only if the 
Department hires more skilled, experienced and scientific staff and undertakes more research 
projects of significance having impact on health and well being of Indian population. 
(Para 2.27 ibid) 
 
Action Taken 
 
4.5.2 Continuous efforts are being made by the Department to increase research work in 
VRDLs, MRUs, MRHRUs thereby enhance their absorption capacity.  So far, 136 VRDLs, 97 
MRUs and 30 MRHRUs have been established and proposals for setting up more such units are  
under process.  Due to diversion of resources and staff for COVID -19 duties to augment the 
COVID testing capacity of the country lead to under utilization of funds. With the COVID 
pandemic on decline, research activities of are expected to increase, resul ting in more 
absorption capacity. The implementing agencies are also being pursued constantly by holding 
review meetings and workshops to expedite the utilization of funds. 
 
4.5.3 Taking into account the pandemic situation, some more centers of ICMR like O ne Health 
Center Nagpur, NIV Units at Chandigarh, Bangalore, Jabalpur & Dibrugarh are under 
construction. These Centers will cater the enhanced need of the Country and will also increase 
the absorption capacity of ICMR. 
 
 
4.6  Allocation as per originally conceived plan 
 
Recommendation 
 
4.6.1 The Committee believes that appropriate expenditure as per originally conceived plan by 
ICMR-DHR would make a good case for seeking higher budgetary allocation at the RE stage 
and BE 2023 -24 as it is well established t hat only through the in -depth health research, the 

30 
 
country can be saved from the life-threatening non-communicable and communicable diseases. 
 
(Para 4.6 ibid) 
 
Action Taken 
 
4.6.2 Guidance of Committee is noted. Also, at the time of RE 2022 -23, an analysis  of last six 
months expenditure figures will be done and based on actual expenditure incurred, RE 2022 -23 
& BE 2023-24 will be demanded. 
 
4.7  Performance evaluation of ICMR 
 
Recommendation 
 
4.7.1 The Committee notes that the external evaluation and analysis conducted by Thomson 
Reuters for ICMR wherein ICMR was compared to similar organizations of US, UK, Australia, 
China and Brazil was done six years ago. Considering that since then the world has seen 3 
waves of Covid-19 pandemic, the Committee believes that now is an opportune time for another 
similar external evaluation. The Committee recommends ICMR to conduct such an evaluation 
wherein ICMR is compared to other competitors on parameters like, trends in budgetary 
allocation and utilization, compar ison between public and private investment, utilization 
avenues and research work under taken, health research infrastructure and its development, 
numbers of scientific professionals and clinical researchers, patents filed, number of 
fellowships and grant for research and future outlook. 
(Para 4.19 ibid) 
 
Action Taken 
 
4.7.2 The observation of the Hon’ble Committee is noted for compliance. 
 
 
  

31 
 
RECOMEMNDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS- AT A GLANCE 
 
RAPID RESPONSE TEAMS (RRT) 
 
The Committee appreciates the existence of the multi -disciplinary team consisting 
of epidemiologists, virologists and immunologists at ICMR. The Committee, however, 
intends to convey the Government that the Rapid Response Team (RRT) must be at the 
alert mode to meet any eventualities of Biological and Chemical weapons/warfare, besides 
combating the challenges posed by the outbreak of endemic or pandemic. Such oversight 
body should not only have relevant linkages with clinical operational and clinical research 
institutes but also integrated co -ordination with national decision making body viz., NITI 
Aayog, PMO and Cabinet Secretariat to ward off or keep vigil against any possible 
biological or chemical warfare so that appropriate decision is taken without del ay even of 
an hour. The Committee understands that the Government needs to incorporate the 
component of biological/chemical, deterrence in its national security strategy. 
 
(Para 3.1.4) 
 
PRADHAN MANTRI AYUSHMAN BHARAT HEALTH INFRASTRUCTURE 
MISSION (PM-ABHIM) 
 
 The Committee endows due credence to PM -ABHIM in bridging gaps in public 
health infrastructure especially focused in critical care facilities and primary healthcare. 
The Committee, in this regard, would like to be apprised of appropriation of Rs. 140.00 
Crore during financial year 2021-22 and Rs. 690.00 crore in financial year 2022 -23 and the 
achievement of physical target against the actual expenditure during the said financial 
years.  
        (Para 3.2.3)  
 
FUNDS FOR COVID-19 TO ICMR 
 
 The Committee reiterates its recommendation that the Ministry of Finance must 
allocate DHR at least 0.1% of GDP for health research in the next five years and earmark

combating any future outbreak of disease and meeting health exigencies. 
 
        (Para 3.3.3)

allocated under Emergency Epidemic Preparedness and Response. The delayed delivery of

resulting into more than 5 lakh death during Second Wave of Pandemic Covid -19 are 
testimony to the fact of exhibiting mismanagement of Pandemic Covid-19. All Government 
machinery reached to the point of grinding halt. The Committee understands the 
limitation of DHR over its anticipating capacity in the situation of unpredicted and 
unprecedented global health emergencies. However, the Committee recommends ICMR to

enhance its professional pursuit and operational efficiency to meet any future health 
eventualities of this magnitude or more than this. The Committee further recommends 
ICMR to undertake project to make i n-depth research/studies to predict/pre -hand 
revelation of possible outbreak of Pandemic by adopting the sewage sample test etc. 
 
       (Para 3.4.4)  
 DIVERSION OF MANPOWER AND OTHER RESOURCES 
 
The Committee recommends DHR to formulate the Contingency Plan to combat 
Covid-19 like national health emergencies viz. outbreak of ‘Monkeypox’ for timely and

1.1    Budgetary Allocation of Ministry of Ayush 
Recommendation 
1.1.1 The Committee notes that the allocation of Ministry of Ayush is 3.69% of the Health Budget 
in 2022-23 as against 4.17% of the Health Budget in 2021-22. Instead of a gradual increase over 
the years, this year has witnessed a marked reduction in allocation for the Ministry of Ayush 
compared to the allocation for Ministry  of Health & Family Welfare. The Committee is not 
happy with this reduction in allocation compared to Health Budget and would like to point out 
that the budget of Ministry of Ayush is still lower to 5% of the Health Budget. The Committee is 
of the consider ed view that Ministry of Ayush, intending to embark on a journey of AYUSH 
revolution, must be adequately funded and schemes meticulously executed so as to realize the 
full potential of AYUSH Systems. The importance of Ayush Systems, particularly in Covid t imes, 
is highly appreciated with rising popularity of these systems and their increasing acceptability as 
an economical and effective system of medicine. The Committee in its 128 th Report had 
emphasized upon appropriate financial support and had also recommended that 10% of the 
Health Budget should be given to Ministry of Ayush from 2022 -23 onwards. The Committee, 
accordingly, recommends that Ministry of Finance maybe approached to allocate atleast 8% of 
the Health Budget to Ministry of Ayush in RE 2022 -23 and 10% of the Health Budget from next 
financial year. 
(Para 2.10 of 136th Report) 
Action Taken 
1.1.2 The projected demand for the financial year 2022 -23 is Rs. 3139.53 crore against which an 
amount of Rs. 3050.00 crore has been allocated. Since projected demand is low due to the reasons 
explained in para 2.2 & 2.4 above, therefore, the allocation for Ministry of Ayush budget comes 
to only 3.67% of Health Ministry‟s budget. How ever, additional fund if any, will be demanded at 
RE stage after due examination. The recommendation of the Committee is noted and the ministry 
is actively considering the concern of the Committee. 
1.2    Realistic assessment of its funds requirement 
 Recommendation 
1.2.1 The Committee, while referring to „Meeting the targets through enhanced allocation of 
budget in the document proposal to 15 th Finance Commission of India on Promotion of AYUSH 
Services & Strengthen the Healthcare Delivery in the country, recommends the Ministry of Ayush  
to have a realistic assessment of its funds requirement keeping in view the larger objectives of the 
Ministry on holistic wellness based on the principles of prevention o f diseases and promotion of 
health with enhanced investment which will in turn reduce the out of pocket expenditure and 
financial burden on the population.  
(Para 2.13 ibid) 
 

3 
 
Action Taken 
1.2.2       Union Cabinet has approved Rs. 3399.35 Crore ( Rs. 2209.58 Crore as Central Share 
and Rs. 1189.77 Crore as State Share) for operationalization of  12,500 Ayush Health and 
Wellness Centres (HWCs) under Ayushman Bharat in a phased manner by from the year 2019 -20 
to 2023 -24.  The objective of AYUSH Health and  Wellness Centres (HWCs) is to establish a 
holistic wellness model based on AYUSH principles and practices, to empower masses for “self -
care” to reduce the disease burden, out of pocket expenditure and to provide informed choice to 
the needy public. The li fe style changes have been also targeted through operationalization of 
12,500 AYUSH Health Wellness Centres. Further, 7553 AYUSH HWCs have been approved 
from 2019 -20 to 2021 -22. Out of this, 3313 AYUSH HWCs have been made functional under 
progressive category. The recommendation of the Committee is noted and the ministry is actively 
considering the concern of the Committee. 
1.3    Construction Projects 
Recommendation 
1.3.1 The Committee observes with concern that except for NIH, Kolkata, Phase II, all the 
remaining construction projects are incomplete. The physical progress as on 31 st December, 
2021 for NIUM, Ghaziabad (73.96%), NIH, Narela (78.20%), AIIA, Sarita Vihar, Ph -II (54%), 
NISARG GRAM, NIN, Pune (74.34%) and NEIAH, Shillong, Ph -II (83.66%) and lik ely date of 
completion for these projects is 31st March,2022. The completion date for AIIA, Goa is 31.12.22 
and physical progress is 73.08%.  The Committee is surprised to find the NIL physical progress 
with respect to NIA, Panchkula wherein the completion  date is 30.06.22 and only Rs 10.68 
crore has been spent out of Rs. 85.67 crore. The Committee would like to be apprised of the 
reasons for NIL physical progress of NIA, Panchkula. The Committee is of the view that the 
construction of these projects should  not be delayed as it may lead to time and cost overruns. 
The Committee recommends the Ministry to give attention to the infrastructure developments 
and closely monitor the progress made in the projects on a monthly basis and complete them in 
a time bound manner so that the Ministry is able to realize its vision 2047 smoothly. The 
Committee hopes that construction projects having the deadline till 31 st March, 2022 are 
completed within the same. 
(Para 2.17 ibid) 
Action Taken 
1.3.2 The project of NIH, Kolkata  Ph-II was completed in Oct, 2021. The other projects i.e. 
NIUM- Ghaziabad, NIH-Narela, AIIA-Sarita Vihar Ph -II, NISARG GRAM – NIN Pune, AIIA-
Goa and NEIAH – Shillong were likely to be completed by March, 2022, but due to various 
reasons viz. Covid -19 pandemic, ban imposed by NGT etc. the work could not be completed in 
scheduled time and shall be completed by the end of 2022 except NIA, Panchkula which is 
expected to be completed by the end of 2023. 
1.3.3 The project of NIA, Panchkula is delayed due to obt aining NOC from Station Headquarter, 
Chandi Mandir, M/o Defence as the land allotted to NIA, Panchkula is adjacent of Station 
Headquarter, Chandi Mandir, Panchkula. The NOC was   granted by  Defence Authorities for 
Construction of NIA on 18 -1-2020. Further, delay is due to various clearances pending with the 
statutory authorities and now most of the clearances have been obtained.   Now, the Construction 
Activities are in full swing.

1.5     UCs of National Ayush Mission 
Recommendation 
1.5.1 The Committee observes that maximum number of UCs of National Ayush Mission followed 
by National Medicinal Plants Board are  pending. Despite Ministry‟s efforts for liquidation of 
UCs with having one to one meetings with concerned States/UTs and also having a dedicated 
web portal for facilitating online submission of UCs, not much difference has been made. Even 
though 34 States /UTs have submitted their State Annual Action Plans through the web portal, 
only 13 States/UTs have submitted UCs online. As regards NMPB, the Committee believes that 
merely issuing periodical reminders is not bearing the desired results. The Committee, th erefore, 
recommends to the Ministry to tackle this problem on priority basis to pursue the concerned 
States/UTs proactively and persuade them to use the web portal for easy and quick submission of 
UCs. The Committee feels that the Ministry should appoint a  nodal officer for the purpose who 
regularly follows up and interact with the nodal officers in the States/UTs for the purpose. 
(Para 2.34 ibid) 
Action Taken  
1.5.2 As of now, 20 State/UT Governments have submitted utilization certificates through the 
NAM web portal and submission by the remaining States/UTs is under process. Ministry of 
Ayush is continuously pursuing the States/UTs to submit the utilization certifica tes through the 
NAM web portal.    
1.5.3 With respect to implementation of NAM Scheme, a dedicated CPMU is established in the 
Ministry having provision of Programme Manager, Consultants, Finance Manager and Accounts 
Manager, etc. for monitoring the impleme ntation of NAM scheme including submission of 
Utilization Certificates. In this regard, States/UTs have been allocated among CPMU members 
for continuous follow up with States/UTs for implementation of NAM Scheme and submission 
of Utilization Certificates. Further, the officers of the NAM Cell are also pursuing with 
States/UTs to expedite the liquidation of UCs. 
1.5.4   For early liquidation of the pending UCs, NMPB has taken the following steps: 
Regional-cum-Facilitation Centres (RCFCs) have given the mandate to co -ordinate with 
reference to liquidation of pending UCs with respective States in addition to periodic Review 
meetings with Project Investigators.  Nodal Officers are also designated for each States/UTs to 
coordinate with them for early liquidation of pending UCs. The liquidation of Pending UCs has 
been given priority and the liquidation status are  monitored on weekly basis, in Senior officers 
Meeting headed by Secretary (Ayush).

3.13    Quality Control of Ayush Drugs 
Recommendation 
3.13.1 The Committee takes cognizance of the major steps taken by the Ministry with intent to 
improve and strengthen quality control of Ayush drugs in the year 2021 and appreciates that the 
Ministry is making efforts for quality control of AYUSH drugs. The Committee comments that 65 
Drug testing labo ratories have been approved under Rule 160 -A to J of the Drugs & 
Cosmetics Rules, 1945 for the testing of Ayurveda, Siddha & Unani drugs, 30 Ayurvedic Drug 
Manufacturing Units have been granted WHO –GMP (CoPP) till date. Moreover,  e-aushadhi 
portal aims at promoting transparency and uniformity in the enforcement of regulatory 
provisions. The Committee notes that as of now 34 State Licensing Authorities, 180 State Drug 
Inspectors and about 1550 Ayush drug manufacturers from 29 States have already registered o n 
the portal for ensuring transparency and uniformity in the enforcement of regulatory provision.

Homoeopathy has been established by merging the HPL and PLIM and expects that the 
Commission can act effectively as the Central Commission Drug Testing Appellate Laboratory.

upholding quality of Ayush drugs, however, the Committee is apprehensive over the temporary 
arrangements made without the incumbents in place. The Committee, accordingly, recommends 
the Ministry to firm up its regulatory framework to ensure that quality of ASU drugs is not 
compromised and ASU drugs get global recognition and acceptance.

VISION DOCUMENTS 
1. Vision Document  of CCRAS  envisages to develop scientific evidence in Ayurvedic 
Principles, drug therapies by way of integrating ancient wisdom with modern technology and to 
bring Ayurveda to the people through innovations related diagnostics, preventive, promotive as 
well as trea tment methods and also introduce scientific research for sustained availability of 
quality natural resources, to translate them into products and processes and in synergy with 
concerned organizations to introduce these innovations into public health systems.  
2. The main features  are Translation of research outcome into clinical practice through 
commercialization of new drugs developed by CCRAS through translational research for making 
them accessible to the public; Mainstreaming of Ayurveda therapies throu gh integration and 
including them in a National Health Programme;  Integration of Ayurveda in National 
Reproductive and Child Health Programme  by developing evidence based Ayurvedic 
interventions for Ante Natal, Post Natal and Child Health Care; Development of new 
drugs/combinations based on the leads from classical literature and also from local health 
traditions on different conditions to meet the demand of unmet medical needs;Development of 
safe /effective products for diseases of national and global impo rtance as add -on/ adjuvant 
therapies and also for standalone management for improvement of quality of life;Generation of 
scientific evidence on safety of Ayurvedic formulations and therapies; Development of the 
Directives addressing different research needs  viz. i. Drug development (addressing issues of 
quality, shelf life, safety issues and other requirements), ii. Safety evaluation (pre -clinical) and 
iii. Clinical research for AYUSH interventions; Validation of Fundamental principles of 
Ayurveda including Ayurveda biology; Development of comprehensive, pragmatic, adaptable an 
Ayurvedic user‟s friendly format for clinical diagnosis and clinical examination for utilization 
among health care professionals and its validation;  Development and validation of Clini cal 
Decision Support Systems and HIMS and e -management; Development of Standard Ayurvedic 
terminologies and its publication in different volume in a phased manner; Occupational Health  
such as Generalized Anxiety Disorder/Stress etcAnd Outreach programmes f or extending health 
care and documentation and institutional linkages with reputed institutes such as CSIR and 
ICMR collaboration 
 
3. The Council has strived to actualize research in most of the areas envisaged in the Vision 
Document 2030 . The Council has  validated Ayurveda classical formulations in identified 
disease conditions to generate tangible evidence on their clinical safety and efficacy and 
undertaken drug development in various identified disease conditions such as Ayush PJ -7 in 
Dengue, Ayush SL in chronic lymphedema, Ayush D in Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus, Carctol S in 
Ovarian Cancer, Ayush HR &Ayush M3 in  Essential Hypertension, C1 oil for wound healing, 
Ayush Manas in Cognitive deficit etc which are under different phases of drug development. The 
Council developed Ayurveda formulations viz.AYUSH  64 , Ayush SG (ShunthiGuggulu) , 
Ayush 82 and transferred their technology through NRDC for making them accessible to the 
public. Also, AYUSH 64 was repurposed for the management of asymptomatic, mild to 
moderate COVID -19 based on the tangible evidence generated through robust studies and made 
available to the public through technology transfer. The Council has also undertaken studies to 
evaluate the clinical efficacy of Ayurveda formulations in Occupatio nal stress in IT 
persons/Nurses.

4. Envisioning the integration of Ayurveda into the National Reproductive and Child Health
